The anomalous traffic comes from **AWS-owned IP ranges** (13.x, 18.x, 34.x, 44.x, 3.x, 15.206.x, 46.137.x, 52.x, 98.80.x) organized into tight synchronized bursts with suspiciously **round per-IP request counts** — a textbook distributed/scripted load pattern:

Evidence strongly supports a **coordinated, scripted/distributed attack**, not organic traffic or a monitoring glitch:

{"id": "60cdf401-5bc2-4ccb-b637-e85b44566869", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "Both subagents are done, so I'm piecing together a timeline from their findings. In the baseline period from midnight to 3am UTC, traffic held steady around 155-160 allowed requests per 5 minutes with zero blocks, consistent with legitimate traffic plus Route53 health checks from known IPs and JA3 fingerprints.

Then from 3:15-3:45 I see a surge peaking at 787 allows at 03:20, tied to a single spoofed Chrome TLS fingerprint distributed across a dozen AWS IPs with suspiciously uniform request counts. This surge contains 160 reflected-XSS attempts on the search endpoint and 320 requests to /admin/dashboard, both matched by WAF rules in count-only mode so they passed through to origin unblocked.

From 03:55-04:04 there's a tight burst of 132 blocks in about 90 seconds from seven AWS IPs, each contributing exactly 13 blocks — mostly SQLi payloads caught by the managed rule set.

Now I'm cataloging the remaining blocks: 10 KnownBadInputs hits on /.env, and 80 extended-pattern matches that only co-occurred with already-blocked SQLi rather than acting independently. By 04:30 everything returns to baseline.

Putting this together, I'm confident this was a genuine coordinated attack — the single consistent TLS fingerprint absent from baseline traffic accounts for essentially all the anomalous activity, which rules out this being organic or misconfigured traffic.

The attacker profile points to someone operating across dozens of AWS-owned IPs spanning seven countries (US, IE, SG, JP, IN, BR, AU), all sharing the identical JA3/JA4 fingerprint and a spoofed Chrome 125 user-agent, firing synchronized sub-minute bursts with suspiciously round request counts like 90, 140, and 13 — clearly scripted rather than human-driven. I'm noting the specific IPs tied to the XSS/admin probing set, including 3.237.25.20 and 44.222.190.x, to document the infrastructure behind this campaign.

The attack itself was multi-vector: reflected XSS payloads thrown at /search?q= using script tags, SVG onload tricks, and iframe injections; classic SQL injection attempts against /login?id= and /search?q= ranging from basic auth bypass strings to UNION-based data extraction and even xp_cmdshell execution attempts; plus reconnaissance probes hitting /.env and /admin/dashboard. Checking whether any of this reached the origin server, I can confirm the WAF successfully blocked every single SQLi and KnownBadInputs attempt — all 132 of them stopped cold before touching the backend.

However, I found two gaps: 160 reflected-XSS requests slipped through because that rule is set to COUNT mode instead of BLOCK, and 320 /admin/dashboard enumeration attempts passed because the rate-limiting rule for sensitive URIs is also COUNT-only and never crossed its threshold. The problem is I can't verify what the origin actually did with these — the response code field is empty across all 4,683 records, so I know the payloads reached the origin but have no visibility into whether the server reflected the XSS or served up admin pages; that would require pulling CloudFront or application-level logs instead.

I'm weighing whether chasing those origin-side logs is worth it. # Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden WAFv2 WebACL response-id-on-page with two Count→Block changes via a single update_web_acl call: remove the CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS and CrossSiteScripting_BODY RuleActionOverrides on the Common Rule Set (Priority 201), and change the custom-sensitive-uri-rate rate-based rule (Priority 450) Action from Count to Block.

## Reasoning
On 2026-09-08 03:00–04:30 UTC an automated multi-vector attack reached the origin because two WebACL settings were in observe-only (Count) mode: XSS overrides let 160 reflected-XSS requests through, and custom-sensitive-uri-rate (Count-only) let 320 /admin/dashboard enumeration requests through. SQLi and Known-Bad-Inputs were already correctly blocked. Switching these two settings to enforcing closes the specific gaps. update_web_acl replaces the entire Rules array and uses an optimistic LockToken that rotates on every write, so the plan re-fetches the token immediately before applying and captures a full-config rollback baseline first. DefaultAction (Allow) stays unchanged.

## Code Change Specification

# Investigation Summary ## Symptoms ### WAF block-volume spike on response-id-on-page **Description:** Block volume on WebACL `response-id-on-page` (CloudFront, protecting website.a.example.com) jumped on 2026-09-08 between ~03:00–04:30 UTC versus the preceding baseline. **Time:** 2026-09-08T03:00:00Z - 2026-09-08T04:30:00Z ## Findings ### Cause: XSS and extended-SQLi attack traffic passed through to origin due to Count-mode rules **Description:** During the incident window (2026-09-08 03:00–04:30 UTC) on WebACL `response-id-on-page`, WAF logs show only **132 requests were actually BLOCKED** (122 by `AWS-AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet`, 10 by `AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet`). Meanwhile attack signals matched rules configured in **Count** mode and were **ALLOWED through to the origin**: `CrossSiteScripting_QueryArguments` fired 160 times (Count → passed), `SQLiExtendedPatterns_QueryArguments_RC_COUNT` fired 80 times (Count → passed). The default action is ALLOW, and 4,551 requests terminated on `Default_Action` ALLOW. This **confirms the earlier hypothesis**: because the XSS CRS overrides and some SQLi extended patterns are set to Count rather than Block, malicious requests matched detection but reached the origin. **Cascades to:** symptom-block-spike #### Gaps - **Origin response impact unconfirmable — edge/origin logging all disabled:** Whether the origin actually served/reflected the allowed-through requests (HTTP 200 vs 4xx/5xx) cannot be determined from current telemetry. WAF responsecodesent is NULL for all 4,683 incident records because the matching rules were in Count mode (non-terminating). CloudFront standard access logs AND real-time logs are DISABLED on distribution EON6JQ4OCGOV7; ALB access logs are DISABLED on HttpEchoAlb; the httpecho origin (EC2 target group) has no CloudWatch app log group. The authoritative source would be ALB access logs (elb_status_code/target_status_code) or CloudFront access/real-time logs — none were enabled during the window, so no retroactive query is possible. Because the origin is an HTTP-echo application, any 200 it served would by design reflect the submitted XSS payload into the response body, so the exposure should be treated as real pending log evidence. ### Root Cause: WAF rules misconfigured in Count mode allowed attack traffic to origin **Description:** The fundamental cause: CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS (Common Rule Set) and custom-sensitive-uri-rate (/admin) are set to **Count/override**, not Block.
